replies.author: @HolidayOrHome
replies.text: @Raquel-vj4uu Well said. Germany is a country where remembering the past is a living part of the culture: memorials, museums and school visits are common here. And at the same time there is so much more to see, from forests to small towns to everyday life. Having traveled a lot ourselves, we’ve learned that the best way to approach any country is without prejudice and with an open mind. Every person deserves that chance, wherever they come from. 🇩🇪

replies.author: @Soulmidwife1111
replies.text: @charlesgrant-skiba5474 Beautifully stated. Thank you.

replies.author: @charlesgrant-skiba5474
replies.text: I believe that the war, Nazi terror, and concentration camps—as well as the Allied bombing of German cities, which claimed the lives of hundreds of thousands of civilians, mostly women and children—belong to the past, to a different country that ceased to exist long ago. The same applies to the slaughter of the indigenous peoples of the Americas or the enslavement of Africans forced to work by plantation owners in the United States; these phenomena relate to an era and to people who are long gone. The six years of the Second World War cannot outweigh nearly two thousand years of civilization and culture in the lands that are now Germany. We must draw lessons from the past and build a better future.

replies.author: @Raquel-vj4uu
replies.text: I think the point of this documentary was to shine a different light on a country that is predominantly known for its dark past. In fact, if asked what Germany is known for, the first answer most people would give is WW2. This documentary is highlighting the fact that there is more to Germany than just that.

replies.author: @HappyTravel99
replies.text: Thank you for your thoughtful and honest feedback. You raise a very important point. The concentration camps and the atrocities of the Nazi era are an undeniable part of Germany's history, and they should never be forgotten. While this documentary focuses primarily on Germany's landscapes, culture, and everyday life, we understand that acknowledging its darker history is equally important. We appreciate you bringing this up, and we'll take your feedback seriously in future documentaries.

comments.author: @BeyondTheMapTV1
comments.text: Germany’s relationship with work is more nuanced than the stereotype of endless productivity suggests. 🇩🇪🌲 Efficiency often means protecting the boundary between working time and private life rather than simply working longer hours. Traditions like Feierabend make sense in that context: productivity and rest are treated as complementary rather than contradictory.
